payload.text: Explain token caching in about 100 words. Use no tools.

data.text: Token caching stores previously processed text representations so repeated requests can reuse them instead of recomputing the same work. In language-model systems, a prompt’s stable prefix may be cached, reducing latency and sometimes lowering input-processing costs. For example, instructions or conversation history that remain unchanged can be reused while only new text is processed. Caches typically have expiration limits, size limits, and rules about which content qualifies. They may be exact-match and sensitive to even small changes. Caching improves efficiency, but developers should consider privacy, invalidation, stale data, and whether cached content could expose information across users or sessions.

payload.text: Give one example of token caching paying off, in about 100 words. Use no tools.

data.text: A customer-support chatbot receives thousands of requests using the same 2,000-token policy manual and product catalog, followed by a short customer question. Without caching, the system repeatedly processes the entire manual and catalog for every request. With token caching, the unchanged policy and catalog prefix is processed once, then reused across requests. The model only needs to process each new question and conversation-specific details. This can make responses faster and reduce input-processing costs, especially during busy periods. The benefit is greatest when prompts share a large, stable prefix and the cached information changes infrequently.
